newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ to merge two ministries, study service sell-off.
newsitem.headline: NZ to merge two ministries, study service sell-off.

text.p: New Zealand on Tuesday detailed plans to create a Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry through the merger of the two existing ministries.

Lockwood Smith, already minister for both forestry and agriculture, said the merger would save costs as services that were increasingly related were combined. He signalled that key inspection services might be sold off.
"The merger is aimed at tighter coordination of government services to the vitally important agriculture, forestry and horticulture sectors," Smith told a news conference.
He said the merger's cost of about NZ$4 million would be paid back within two to six years through cost savings once the new structure is operational by March 1 next year.
At the same time, the government will also study if some functions of the agriculture ministry's service arm could be moved to the private sector.
"Some commercial services may be transferred to a crown company or state-owned enterprise operation and be opened to potential competition from the private sector," Smith said.
Any decisions on commercialisation would be made by the end of the year, he noted.
Areas that will be reviewed include front line meat inspection services, which conduct extensive quality checks in the export-dominated lamb, beef and sheepmeat industries.
However, Smith said any changes proposed in this area would first have to be agreed by New Zealand's trading partners.
"Longer term, while the government has to ensure meat inspection standards are met, it doesn't have to employ the inspector who actually looks at the carcass," he said.
Meat industry products are New Zealand's largest export income earner, accounting for one dollar in every six earned overseas.
Major markets include the United States, Canada and South Korea for beef, and European Union states, led by Britain, for lamb and mutton.
"Opening up inspection to the private sector could help drive down costs for meat companies as they would be able to directly manage the costs involved," Smith said.
